text: “You would not believe how encouraged we are, Dmitri Fyodorovich, by this readiness of yours ... ,” Nikolai Parfenovich started saying, with an animated look and with visible pleasure shining in his big, protruding, pale gray, and, by the way, extremely myopic eyes, from which he had just removed his spectacles a moment before.
explanation: Nikolai Parfenovich expresses extreme encouragement and visible pleasure seen in his big, pale, myopic eyes, which he'd just removed his glasses from at Dmitri Fyodorovich's Mitya's willingness to cooperate.

text: “And you have made a very just observation concerning our mutual confidentiality, without which it is sometimes even impossible to proceed in matters of such importance, in the case and sense that the suspected person indeed wishes, hopes, and is able to vindicate himself.
explanation: Nikolai Parfenovich agrees that Mitya's point about mutual confidentiality is correct, stating that such discretion is essential in serious cases where the suspected individual is trying to prove his innocence.

text: For our part, we shall do everything possible, and you have already been able to see how we are conducting this case ...
explanation: He promises that they the investigators/officials will do their best, implying Mitya has already witnessed their appropriate handling of the investigation.

text: Do you approve, Ippolit Kirillovich?” he suddenly turned to the prosecutor.
explanation: He abruptly asks the prosecutor, Ippolit Kirillovich, for his approval of the way the case is being handled.

text: “Oh, indubitably,” the prosecutor approved, though somewhat drily compared with Nikolai Parfenovich’s outburst.
explanation: The prosecutor agrees, using the word "indubitably" undoubtedly, but his response lacks the enthusiasm shown by Nikolai Parfenovich.

text: I will note once and for all that the newly arrived Nikolai Parfenovich, from the very beginning of his career among us, felt a marked respect for our Ippolit Kirillovich, the prosecutor, and became almost heart-to-heart friends with him.
explanation: The narrator interjects to state that Nikolai Parfenovich the newly arrived official immediately developed deep respect for the prosecutor, Ippolit Kirillovich, leading to a close friendship.

text: He was almost the only man who believed without reservation in the remarkable psychological and oratorical talents of our “passed-over” Ippolit Kirillovich, and also fully believed that he had indeed been passed over.
explanation: Nikolai Parfenovich was nearly the sole person who genuinely trusted in the superior mind-reading and public-speaking abilities of Ippolit Kirillovich who had supposedly been overlooked for promotion.

text: He had heard of him while still in Petersburg.
explanation: Nikolai Parfenovich had known of the prosecutor's reputation even before coming to the area.

text: And in turn the young Nikolai Parfenovich happened to be the only man in the whole world whom our “passed-over” prosecutor came sincerely to love.
explanation: Reciprocally, the prosecutor sincerely loved the young Nikolai Parfenovich, who was unique in this regard.

text: On the way there they had had time to set up a few things and make arrangements for the impending case, and now, at the table, the sharp little mind of Nikolai Parfenovich caught on the wing and understood every indication, every movement in the face of his older colleague, from half a word, a look, a wink of the eye.
explanation: During their journey, they had already coordinated details for the case, and now, as they sat together, Nikolai Parfenovich's quick intelligence allowed him to instantly grasp his senior colleague's thoughts, even from the smallest non-verbal cues.

text: “Gentlemen, give me leave to tell my own story and do not interrupt me with trifles, and I will lay it all out for you in no time,” Mitya was seething.
explanation: Mitya, agitated, insists that the officials allow him to narrate his entire story uninterrupted by insignificant details, promising to finish quickly.

text: “Excellent, sir.
explanation: Nikolai Parfenovich agrees to Mitya's request.

text: Thank you.
explanation: He expresses gratitude.

text: But before we go on to hear your account, allow me simply to mention one more little fact, of great interest for us, namely, the ten roubles you borrowed yesterday, at around five o’clock, by pawning your pistols to your friend Pyotr Ilyich Perkhotin.”
explanation: However, before Mitya begins, Nikolai Parfenovich wishes to mention a highly relevant detail: Mitya's action of borrowing ten roubles from his friend Perkhotin by pawning his pistols around five o'clock the previous day.

text: “I pawned them, gentlemen, I pawned them for ten roubles, that’s all.
explanation: Mitya confirms that he pawned his pistols for ten roubles and nothing more.

text: What of it?
explanation: He challenges the relevance of the fact.

text: As soon as I got back to town from my trip, I pawned them at once.”
explanation: He states that the pawning occurred immediately upon his return to town from a trip.

text: “Got back?
explanation: Nikolai Parfenovich questions Mitya, noting that his phrasing implies a return.

text: So you left town?”
explanation: He clarifies by asking if Mitya had been out of town.

text: “I did, gentlemen, I went thirty miles out of town, didn’t you know that?”
explanation: Mitya confirms that he had traveled thirty miles outside of town and expresses surprise that the officials were unaware of this.

text: The prosecutor and Nikolai Parfenovich exchanged glances.
explanation: The two officials look at each other, signaling shared acknowledgment or surprise at Mitya's admission.

text: “Suppose you begin your story with a systematic description of your whole day yesterday, starting from the morning?
explanation: The official suggests Mitya begin his account by systematically describing everything that happened the previous day, starting in the morning.

text: Let us know, for example, why you left town, and precisely when you went and came back ... and all these facts ...”
explanation: He specifies that Mitya should include his reasons for leaving town, the exact times of his departure and return, and all related events.

text: “But you should have asked me that from the very beginning,” Mitya laughed loudly, “and, if you please, I should start not from yesterday but from the day before yesterday, from that morning; then you’ll understand where, how, and why I went or drove.
explanation: Mitya laughs, pointing out that this detail should have been asked earlier, and suggests that for a proper understanding, he needs to start his narrative from the morning of the day before yesterday.

text: The day before yesterday, gentlemen, I went to a local merchant, Samsonov, to borrow three thousand roubles from him on the best security—a sudden itch, gentlemen, a sudden itch...”
explanation: He begins his story by stating that two days prior, he visited the merchant Samsonov to borrow three thousand roubles against good collateral, driven by a sudden, intense impulse the "itch".

text: “Allow me to interrupt you,” the prosecutor interjected politely, “why did you so suddenly need precisely that amount, that is, three thousand roubles? “
explanation: The prosecutor politely breaks in to ask why Mitya suddenly needed the exact sum of three thousand roubles.

text: “Eh, gentlemen, why pick on such little things: how, when, and why, and precisely this much money and not that much, and all that claptrap ... if you keep on, it’ll take you three volumes and an epilogue to cram it all in.”
explanation: Mitya dismisses the question as nitpicking over minor details the logistics of the need, the specific amount, claiming that continuing such detailed inquiries would require an impossibly long account.

text: All this Mitya said with the good-natured but impatient familiarity of a man who wishes to tell the whole truth and is full of the best intentions.
explanation: The narrator notes that Mitya spoke with a friendly but restless confidence, characteristic of someone sincere and eager to tell the complete truth.

text: “Gentlemen,” he caught himself, as it were, “don’t murmur against me for my bristliness.
explanation: Mitya checks his behavior and asks the officials not to criticize his impatience or irritability.

text: I ask you again: believe once more that I feel the utmost respect and fully understand the situation.
explanation: He reiterates his deep respect for them and his full awareness of the circumstances.

text: And don’t think that I’m drunk.
explanation: He assures them he is not intoxicated.

text: I’ve sobered up now.
explanation: He states he is currently sober.

text: And it would be no hindrance if I were drunk, because: Sober and wise, he’s stupid, Drunk and stupid, he’s wise.
explanation: He adds that even if he were drunk, it wouldn't matter, citing a paradoxical saying that a person is stupid when sober/wise, but wise when drunk/stupid.

text: That’s how I am.
explanation: He claims this paradox applies to him.

text: Ha, ha!
explanation: He laughs.

text: I see, by the way, that it’s not proper for me to be cracking jokes with you yet—that is, before we’ve explained everything.
explanation: He realizes that joking is inappropriate until the facts have been established.

text: Allow me to keep my dignity.
explanation: He asks for permission to maintain his composure.

text: I quite understand the present difference: I’m still sitting before you as a criminal, and, therefore, unequal to you in the highest degree, and your duty is to watch me:
explanation: He acknowledges the power imbalance, recognizing that he is currently viewed as a criminal, making him fundamentally unequal to them, and that they are obligated to observe him closely.

text: you really can’t pat me on the back for Grigory, one certainly can’t go breaking old men’s heads with impunity, you’ll probably try me and lock me up for, what, six months or a year in the penitentiary for that, or, I don’t know, whatever the sentence would be—but without loss of rights, it will be without loss of rights, won’t it, prosecutor?
explanation: He admits they cannot overlook the attack on Grigory breaking an old man's head, accepting that he will likely face a trial and a sentence perhaps six months to a year in prison, but anxiously seeks confirmation from the prosecutor that he will retain his civil rights.

text: And so, gentlemen, I quite understand this difference ...
explanation: He summarizes by confirming his understanding of the difference in status.

text: But you must also agree that you could confuse even God himself with such questions: where I stepped, how I stepped, when I stepped, what I stepped in?
explanation: He argues that the officials' overly detailed questions e.g., about his movements and timing are so minute that they could confuse anyone.

text: I’ll get confused that way, and you’ll pick up every dropped stitch and write it down at once, and what will come of it?
explanation: He fears becoming confused, which would allow them to immediately record any inconsistencies, leading to no positive outcome.

text: Nothing will come of it!
explanation: He concludes that this method will be fruitless.

text: And finally, since I’ve already begun telling my tale, I’ll finish it now, and you, gentlemen, being most noble and highly educated, will forgive me.
explanation: He states his intention to finish his story, trusting that the noble and educated officials will overlook his bluntness.

text: I’ll end precisely with a request: you, gentlemen, must unlearn this official method of interrogation, I mean, first you begin, say, with something measly and insignificant: how did you get up, what did you eat, how did you spit, and ‘having lulled the criminal’s attention,’ you suddenly catch him with a stunning question: ‘Whom did you kill, whom did you rob?’
explanation: He requests that they stop using their standard interrogation technique, which involves starting with trivial questions like getting up or eating to deliberately lower the accused's guard before springing a major, incriminating question on them.

text: Ha, ha!
explanation: He laughs.

text: That’s your official method, that’s your rule, that’s what all your cleverness is based on!
explanation: He identifies this as the foundation of their formal, clever interrogation strategy.

text: You can lull peasants with your cleverness, but not me.
explanation: He asserts that while their method might trick less sophisticated people, it won't work on him.

text: I understand the system, I was in the service myself, ha, ha, ha!
explanation: He claims familiarity with their methods because he was once in a similar profession, concluding with laughter.

text: You’re not angry, are you, gentlemen?
explanation: He asks if he has offended them.

text: You’ll forgive my boldness?” he cried, looking at them with almost surprising good-naturedness.
explanation: He asks them to forgive his audacity while looking at them with unexpected good nature.

text: “Mitka Karamazov said it, so it’s excusable, because what would be inexcusable in an intelligent man is excusable in Mitka!
explanation: He excuses his comments by attributing them to his persona, "Mitka Karamazov," suggesting that his foolishness makes his impudence forgivable where an intelligent person's would not be.

text: Ha, ha!”
explanation: He laughs again.

text: Nikolai Parfenovich listened and laughed, too.
explanation: Nikolai Parfenovich, listening to Mitya's outburst, joins in the laughter.

text: The prosecutor, though he did not laugh, was studying Mitya intently, without taking his eyes off him, as if not wishing to miss the least word, the least movement, the least twitch of the least little line on his face.
explanation: The prosecutor, however, did not laugh but instead focused on Mitya intently, meticulously observing every minute detail of his expression and movement.

text: “Incidentally, that is how we began with you from the beginning,” Nikolai Parfenovich replied, still laughing, “not confusing you with questions about how you got up in the morning and what you ate, but beginning even from what is all too essential.”
explanation: Nikolai Parfenovich, still laughing, contradicts Mitya's criticism by stating that they had, in fact, started with truly important matters rather than trivial ones like his morning routine.

text: “I understand, I understood and appreciated it, and I appreciate still more your present kindness to me, which is unprecedented, worthy of the noblest souls.
explanation: Mitya acknowledges and values their kind treatment, which he describes as unique and reflective of noble character.

text: We are three noble men come together here, and let everything with us be on the footing of mutual trust between educated and worldly men, bound by nobility and honor.
explanation: He proposes that since they are all educated, worldly, and honorable men, their interaction should be based on mutual trust.

text: In any case, allow me to look upon you as my best friends in this moment of my life, in this moment when my honor is humiliated!
explanation: He asks permission to view them as his closest friends during this time when his honor is being degraded.

text: That’s no offense to you, is it, gentlemen?”
explanation: He asks if this designation offends them.

text: “On the contrary, you’ve expressed it all quite beautifully, Dmitri Fyodorovich,” Nikolai Parfenovich gravely and approvingly agreed.
explanation: Nikolai Parfenovich solemnly and approvingly assures Mitya that his sentiments were expressed perfectly.

text: “And away with little details, gentlemen, with all these pettifogging details,” Mitya delightedly exclaimed, “otherwise the devil knows what will come of it, isn’t that so?”
explanation: Mitya joyfully urges them to discard all minor, trivial details, arguing that focusing on them will only lead to confusion.

text: “I will follow your sensible advice completely,” the prosecutor suddenly mixed in, addressing Mitya.
explanation: The prosecutor interjects to state that he will fully adhere to Mitya's rational suggestion.

text: However, I still do not withdraw my question.
explanation: He immediately qualifies his agreement by insisting that his previous question remains on the table.

text: It is all too essentially necessary for us to know why precisely you needed such an amount—that is, precisely three thousand.”
explanation: He stresses that it is absolutely vital for the investigation to know the exact reason Mitya needed the precise sum of three thousand roubles.

text: “Why I needed it?
explanation: Mitya repeats the question.

text: Well, for this and that ... well, to repay a debt.”
explanation: He replies vaguely, then specifies he needed the money to pay off a debt.

text: “To whom, precisely?”
explanation: The prosecutor presses for the specific name of the creditor.

text: “That I positively refuse to tell you, gentlemen!
explanation: Mitya unequivocally refuses to disclose the identity of the person.

text: You see, it’s not that I cannot tell you, or don’t dare, or am afraid, because it’s all a paltry matter and perfectly trifling, no, but I won’t tell you on principle: it’s my private life, and I will not allow you to invade my private life.
explanation: He clarifies that his refusal is not due to inability, fear, or the triviality of the debt, but because of a moral principle: the identity of the creditor is part of his private life, which he refuses to let them investigate.

text: That is my principle.
explanation: He stresses that this stance is a matter of principle.

text: Your question is irrelevant to the case, and whatever is irrelevant to the case is my private life!
explanation: He asserts a rule: any question not directly relevant to the case falls into his private domain.

text: I wanted to repay a debt, a debt of honor, but to whom I won’t say.”
explanation: He confirms the debt was a matter of honor but maintains his refusal to name the recipient.

text: “Allow us to write that down,” said the prosecutor.
explanation: The prosecutor asks for permission to record Mitya's refusal.

text: “As you wish.
explanation: Mitya agrees to the recording.

text: Write down this: that I just won’t say.
explanation: He tells them to record his simple refusal to speak.

text: Write, gentlemen, that I would even consider it dishonorable to say.
explanation: He instructs them to also note that revealing the name would be an act of dishonor for him.

text: You’ve got lots of time for writing, haven’t you?”
explanation: He asks sarcastically if they have ample time for all this documentation.

text: “Allow me, dear sir, to caution you and remind you once more, in case you are still unaware of it,” the prosecutor said with particular and rather stern impressiveness, “that you have every right not to answer the questions that are put to you now, and we, on the contrary, have no right to extort answers from you, if you decline to answer for one reason or another.
explanation: The prosecutor solemnly and sternly reminds Mitya that he has the legal right to refuse to answer any questions, and the officials cannot legally force him to reply.

text: That is a matter of your personal consideration.
explanation: He states that the decision to answer is entirely Mitya's to make.

text: On the other hand, in such a situation, it is our business to point out to you and explain the full extent of the harm you will be doing yourself by refusing to give this or that evidence.
explanation: He then states that their duty is to inform Mitya of the potential damage he is inflicting on his own case by withholding crucial testimony.

text: At which point I ask you to continue.”
explanation: Having delivered the warning, the prosecutor asks Mitya to resume his story.

text: “Gentlemen, I’m not angry ... I ... ,” Mitya started mumbling, somewhat taken aback by this reprimand, “you see, gentlemen, this Samsonov to whom I went then ...”
explanation: Mitya, slightly confused and humbled by the prosecutor's formal warning, begins to mumble a defense before resuming his narrative about his visit to Samsonov.

text: We shall not, of course, reproduce his detailed account of what is already known to the reader.
explanation: The narrator decides not to repeat the details of Mitya's story which the reader already knows.

text: The narrator was impatient to tell everything in the smallest particulars, and at the same time to get through it quickly.
explanation: Mitya was eager to share all the minute details but also wanted to rush through the account.

text: But his evidence was being written down as he gave it, and he therefore had necessarily to be stopped.
explanation: Because his testimony was being simultaneously transcribed, Mitya was frequently interrupted by the officials.

text: Dmitri Fyodorovich objected but submitted, was angry, but so far good-naturedly.
explanation: Mitya complained about the interruptions but yielded to the process, expressing his anger in a relatively good-humored way.

text: True, from time to time he cried out, “Gentlemen, this would exasperate the Lord God himself!” or “Gentlemen, do you know you’re irritating me for nothing?” but despite his exclamations, he still preserved his friendly and expansive mood.
explanation: Despite occasional angry outbursts, Mitya generally maintained a friendly and open demeanor.

text: Thus he told them how Samsonov had “hoodwinked” him two days before.
explanation: He recounted how Samsonov had deceived him two days earlier.

text: He now realized fully that he had been hoodwinked then.
explanation: He acknowledged that he now completely understood the deception.

text: The sale of the watch for six roubles in order to get money for the road, which was still completely unknown to the district attorney and the prosecutor, at once aroused their greatest interest, and, to Mitya’s boundless indignation, they found it necessary to record this fact in detail, seeing in it a second confirmation of the circumstance that even a day before he had been almost without a kopeck.
explanation: His story about selling his watch for six roubles for travel money—a fact new to the officials—greatly interested them; despite Mitya's extreme annoyance, they recorded it as a second piece of evidence that he had been nearly penniless the day before.

text: Little by little Mitya was becoming gloomy.
explanation: As the process continued, Mitya gradually became dispirited.

text: Then, having described his trip to Lyagavy, the night spent in the fume-poisoned hut, and so on, he brought his story as far as his return to town, where he began on his own, without being specially asked, to describe in detail his jealous torments over Grushenka.
explanation: After recounting his travels including his time in Lyagavy and the smoky hut, he returned to town in his story and voluntarily started detailing his jealous suffering concerning Grushenka.

text: He was listened to silently and attentively; they particularly went into the circumstance of his having long ago set up his lookout for Grushenka going to Fyodor Pavlovich in Maria Kondratievna’s backyard, and of Smerdyakov’s bringing him information: this was much noticed and written down.
explanation: The officials listened quietly and carefully, paying close attention to and recording the long-standing arrangement Mitya had for watching Grushenka go to Fyodor Pavlovich via a neighbor's yard, as well as Smerdyakov's role in supplying information.

text: Of his jealousy he spoke ardently and extensively, and though inwardly ashamed at displaying his most intimate feelings, so to speak, “for general disgrace,” he obviously tried to overcome his shame for the sake of being truthful.
explanation: He spoke passionately and at length about his jealousy, making an effort to suppress his embarrassment at revealing such private emotions in public for the sake of complete honesty.

text: The indifferent sternness of the district attorney’s and, especially, the prosecutor’s eyes, which they kept fixed on him during his account, disconcerted him in the end rather strongly:
explanation: The cold, severe gaze of the officials, particularly the prosecutor, which was fixed on him throughout his testimony, eventually disturbed him significantly.

text: “This boy, Nikolai Parfenovich, with whom I exchanged some silly remarks about women only a few days ago, and this sickly prosecutor are not worthy of my telling them this,” flashed sadly through his mind.
explanation: A sad thought crossed his mind: that the young Nikolai Parfenovich and the frail prosecutor were not worthy of hearing his intimate confession.

text: “Oh, shame!
explanation: He felt a sense of self-disgrace.

text: Be patient, humble, hold thy peace,’”273 he concluded his thoughts with this line of verse, but still collected himself again in order to go on.
explanation: He ended his self-reflection with a line of poetry urging patience and silence, but nevertheless regained his composure to continue the narrative.

text: Having come to the part about Madame Khokhlakov, he even brightened up again, and was even about to tell a certain recent anecdote, unrelated to the case, concerning the good lady, but the district attorney stopped him and politely suggested that they pass on “to more essential things.”
explanation: When he reached the part of the story involving Madame Khokhlakov, his spirits lifted, and he was about to share a irrelevant anecdote about her, but the district attorney courteously intervened, asking him to focus on more important matters.

text: Finally, having described his despair and told them of that moment when, as he walked out of Madame Khokhlakov’s, he had even had the thought of “quickly putting a knife into someone, just to get the three thousand,” he was stopped again, and it was recorded that “he wanted to put a knife into someone.”
explanation: When he described his desperation after leaving Madame Khokhlakov's, where he thought of quickly stabbing someone just to get the three thousand roubles, the narration was paused so that the incriminating thought could be officially recorded.

text: Mitya let them write it down without protest.
explanation: Mitya allowed this statement to be written down without any objection.

text: Finally he came to the point in the story when he suddenly found out that Grushenka had deceived him and left Samsonov’s just after he brought her there, though she had told him she would stay until midnight.
explanation: He reached the moment in his story where he discovered that Grushenka had lied to him, having left Samsonov’s house immediately after he dropped her off, despite promising to stay until midnight.

text: “If I didn’t kill this Fenya right then, gentlemen, it was only because I had no time,” suddenly escaped him at this place in the story.
explanation: At this point, Mitya impulsively confessed that he had only refrained from killing Fenya a maid because he lacked the time.

text: And this, too, was carefully written down.
explanation: This statement was also meticulously recorded by the officials.

text: Mitya waited gloomily and was beginning to tell how he ran to his; father’s garden, when the district attorney suddenly stopped him, and, opening his large briefcase, which lay beside him on the sofa, took out of it a brass pestle.
explanation: Mitya waited sadly and began to describe running to his father's garden, but the district attorney interrupted him, opened his briefcase, and produced a brass pestle.

text: “Are you familiar with this object?” he showed it to Mitya.
explanation: The district attorney holds up the pestle and asks Mitya if he recognizes it.

text: “Ah, yes!” Mitya grinned gloomily, “indeed I am!
explanation: Mitya confirms his recognition with a gloomy grin.

text: Let me see it ... Or don’t, devil take it!”
explanation: He starts to ask to see it but then abruptly changes his mind, dismissing the object.

text: “You forgot to mention it,” the district attorney observed.
explanation: The district attorney points out that Mitya failed to include the pestle in his testimony.

text: “Ah, the devil!
explanation: Mitya expresses annoyance.

text: I wouldn’t hide it from you, we certainly couldn’t get along without it, don’t you agree?
explanation: He claims he wouldn't have hidden it, suggesting its importance is obvious.

text: It just escaped my memory.”
explanation: He asserts that he simply forgot to mention the pestle.

text: “Be so good, then, as to tell us in detail how you came to arm yourself with it.”
explanation: The official asks him to provide a detailed account of when and why he armed himself with the pestle.

text: “I’ll be so good, if you wish, gentlemen.”
explanation: Mitya sarcastically agrees to comply with the request.

text: And Mitya told how he took the pestle and ran.
explanation: Mitya then recounted the physical action of taking the pestle and running.

text: “But what purpose did you have in mind in arming yourself with such an implement?”
explanation: The official asks for Mitya's deliberate intention in choosing the pestle as a weapon.

text: “What purpose?
explanation: Mitya repeats the question.

text: No purpose!
explanation: He insists he had no specific goal.

text: I just grabbed it and ran.”
explanation: He claims it was an impulsive act—he simply seized it and started running.

text: “But why, if there was no purpose?”
explanation: The official presses him again, asking why he took it if there was no reason.

text: Mitya was seething with vexation.
explanation: Mitya became intensely angry and annoyed.

text: He looked fixedly at the “boy” and grinned gloomily and maliciously.
explanation: He stared at Nikolai Parfenovich the "boy" and gave a dark, spiteful smile.

text: The thing was that he felt more and more ashamed at having just told “such people” the story of his jealousy, so sincerely and with such effusion.
explanation: His increasing shame was rooted in the fact that he had revealed his deep, sincere feelings about his jealousy to people he considered unworthy.

text: “I spit on the pestle,” suddenly escaped him.
explanation: He impulsively uttered a contemptuous phrase about the pestle.

text: “Even so, sir.”
explanation: The official acknowledges his statement without reacting strongly.

text: “So I grabbed it to keep off the dogs.
explanation: Mitya suggests he took the pestle to ward off stray dogs.

text: Or because it was dark ...
explanation: He suggests it was because of the darkness.

text: Or just in case.”
explanation: He offers a final, vague possibility: as a general precaution.

text: “And have you always been in the habit of taking some weapon with you when going out at night, since you are so afraid of the dark?”
explanation: The official asks sarcastically if Mitya routinely carries a weapon at night because he fears the dark.

text: “Agh, the devil, pah!
explanation: Mitya expresses strong frustration.

text: Gentlemen, it’s literally impossible to talk to you!”
explanation: He bursts out that it is truly impossible to communicate with them.

text: Mitya cried out in the utmost annoyance, and turning to the clerk, all red with anger, with a sort of frenzied note in his voice, quickly said to him:
explanation: In his extreme annoyance, Mitya turns toward the court clerk, his face flushed, and speaks quickly in a frantic tone.

text: “Take this down right now ... right now ... ‘that I grabbed the pestle in order to run and kill my father, Fyodor Pavlovich ... by hitting him on the head’!
explanation: He dictates an explicit, incriminating confession to the clerk: that he took the pestle to run and murder his father, Fyodor Pavlovich, by hitting him on the head.

text: Well, are you content now, gentlemen?
explanation: He asks the officials if this confession satisfies them.

text: Does that ease your hearts?” he said, staring defiantly at the prosecutor and the district attorney.
explanation: He stares aggressively at the officials and asks if this admission relieves their minds.

text: “We realize only too well that you have given such evidence just now because you are annoyed with us and vexed by the questions we put to you, which you regard as petty, and which in essence are quite essential,” the prosecutor answered him drily.
explanation: The prosecutor responds flatly, stating that they fully understand Mitya's confession was made out of anger and irritation over questions Mitya considers trivial but which they believe are highly important.

text: “But for pity’s sake, gentlemen!
explanation: Mitya expresses a plea for understanding.

text: So I took the pestle ...
explanation: He acknowledges taking the pestle.

text: So, what does one pick things up for in such cases?
explanation: He asks what anyone would take in a similar situation.

text: I don’t know.
explanation: He says he doesn't know the reason.

text: I snatched it and ran.
explanation: He repeats that it was an impulsive action.

text: That’s all.
explanation: He insists that is the entire explanation.

text: Shame on you, gentlemen—passons, or I swear I won’t say anything more!”
explanation: He expresses shame on them and demands they move on "passons," French for "let's pass/proceed", or he threatens to stop speaking altogether.

text: He leaned his elbow on the table and propped his head in his hand.
explanation: Mitya rests his elbow on the table, supporting his head with his hand.

text: He was sitting sideways to them, looking at the wall, and trying to overcome the bad feeling inside him.
explanation: He positioned himself to face the wall, avoiding the officials, in an attempt to conquer his inner frustration.

text: In fact, he really had a terrible urge to stand up and declare that he was not going to say another word, “even if you should take me out and hang me.”
explanation: He felt an intense desire to stop the interrogation entirely, even if the consequence was execution.

text: “You see, gentlemen,” he suddenly spoke, overcoming himself with difficulty, “you see.
explanation: He speaks again, struggling to control himself.

text: I’m listening to you and imagining ...
explanation: He tells them that as he listens, he is reminded of something he imagines.

text: You see, sometimes I dream a dream in my sleep ... one particular dream, and I often dream it, it keeps repeating itself, that someone is chasing me, someone I’m terribly afraid of is chasing me in the darkness, at night, looking for me, and I’m hiding from him somewhere behind a door or a wardrobe, hiding in a humiliating way, and moreover he knows perfectly well where I’m hiding, but he seems to pretend not to know where I am on purpose, in order to torment me longer, in order to revel in my fear ...
explanation: He describes a recurring nightmare where a feared pursuer chases him in the dark while he hides shamefully behind furniture, and the pursuer knowingly prolongs the torment by pretending not to find him.

text: That’s what you are doing now!
explanation: He equates the officials' interrogation method to the psychological torture in his recurring nightmare.

text: It’s just the same!”
explanation: He insists the feeling is identical.

text: “Is that the sort of dreams you have?” the prosecutor inquired.
explanation: The prosecutor asks if that is his typical kind of dream.

text: “Yes, I have such dreams ...
explanation: Mitya confirms that he has these dreams.

text: Why, do you want to write it down?” Mitya grinned crookedly.
explanation: He asks sarcastically, with a distorted grin, if the dream details are relevant enough for the record.

text: “No, sir, I do not want to write it down, but still you do have curious dreams.”
explanation: The prosecutor assures him he will not write it down but notes that Mitya's dreams are unusual.

text: “This time it’s not a dream!
explanation: Mitya insists that his current situation is not a hallucination or dream.

text: Realism, gentlemen, the realism of actual life!
explanation: He declares the situation to be the harsh reality of life.

text: I’m the wolf, you’re the hunters—so hunt the wolf down.”
explanation: He compares himself to a wolf and the officials to hunters, urging them to proceed with their pursuit.

text: “You shouldn’t make such comparisons ... ,” Nikolai Parfenovich began very gently.
explanation: Nikolai Parfenovich mildly suggests that Mitya should not use such dramatic metaphors.

text: “Why shouldn’t I, gentlemen, why shouldn’t I!” Mitya boiled up again, though he had apparently unburdened his soul with this outburst of sudden anger and was growing kinder again with every word.
explanation: Mitya bursts out passionately again, defending his right to use the comparison, even though this sudden outburst seemed to have relieved his tension and made him more amiable.

text: You may disbelieve a criminal or a prisoner in the dock whom you’re tormenting with your questions, but to disbelieve the noblest man, gentlemen, the noblest impulses of the soul I cry it boldly!—no! that you cannot do ... you even have no right to ... but—
explanation: He argues that while they can distrust an accused person being cross-examined, they cannot, and have no right to, disbelieve a person's bold expression of the soul's noblest intentions.

text: . . . heart, hold thy peace, Be patient, humble, hold thy peace!
explanation: He quotes the line of verse again, urging his own heart to be quiet and patient.

text: Well, shall I go on?” he broke off gloomily.
explanation: He pauses sadly and asks if he should continue his narrative.

text: “Of course, if you’d be so good,” replied Nikolai Parfenovich.
explanation: Nikolai Parfenovich politely encourages Mitya to resume his story.
